lessons.title: Investment Declarations, Proofs and Your Regime Choice

body.text: What you declare in April decides how much tax payroll deducts. What you prove in January decides whether that deduction was right. Declare without proving and the difference lands on your February and March payslips.

children.text: Rahul is a data engineer in Bengaluru earning ₹15,00,000. In April 2026 he ticked "old regime" on his payroll portal, declared rent, tax-saving investments and health insurance, and watched his TDS settle at about ₹6,283 a month. In January 2027, HR asked for proofs. Two of his declarations had no paperwork behind them. His February payslip carried a nasty surprise. This lesson walks through the full declaration cycle, what each claim needs, and how to decide whether the old regime is worth the paperwork at all.

body.title: A typical tax year on the payroll portal

events.title: Choose a regime and declare
events.description: You tell payroll whether you want the old regime and list the rent, investments and payments you plan to make. These are estimates, not proofs.

events.title: TDS based on declarations
events.description: Payroll estimates your annual tax using your declared figures and spreads it across the months, as covered in Lesson 1.

events.title: Proof window
events.description: You upload rent receipts, investment statements and premium receipts along with Form 124 (formerly Form 12BB). Each employer sets its own cut-off date.

events.title: Recalculation
events.description: Payroll replaces declared figures with proven ones. Any shortfall in TDS is recovered from the last one or two salaries.

events.title: Form 130 issued
events.description: Your salary TDS certificate shows only the exemptions and deductions payroll accepted.

events.title: Return filed
events.description: You can still claim genuine deductions payroll missed, as long as you made the payment within the tax year and hold the proof.

children.text: Decide the Regime Before You Declare Anything

Declarations only matter in the old regime. The new regime under Section 202 (formerly 115BAC) ignores almost all of them. So the first question is not "what can I declare?" but "will my declarations add up to enough to beat the new regime's lower slabs?"

body.caption: What each regime lets payroll consider

cells: Allowed for domestic travel, with conditions
Home loan interest on a self-occupied house, Section 22 (formerly 24(b))
Investments such as EPF, PPF, ELSS, life insurance, Section 123 (formerly 80C)
Allowed, up to 14% of basic plus DA
Allowed, up to 10% of basic plus DA
₹25,000 for self and family, plus up to ₹50,000 for senior citizen parents

children.text: Because the new regime has wider, lower slabs and a larger standard deduction, the old regime needs a substantial pile of exemptions and deductions just to break even. The chart shows roughly how much, for a resident below 60 with no other income.

body.title: Exemptions and deductions needed for the old regime to match the new regime

body.caption: Break-even in numbers (tax year 2026-27, beyond the old regime's standard deduction)
headers: Old regime claims needed to match it

children.text: Notice that the break-even stops rising at about ₹8,00,000. Once salary crosses roughly ₹24,75,000, both regimes tax every extra rupee at 30%, so the gap between them stays fixed. Below that, the old regime needs a bigger cushion as salary rises, because the new regime keeps its lower 15%, 20% and 25% slabs for longer.

body.title: Quick Check: Is the Old Regime Worth It?
body.question: Farhan earns ₹20,00,000. In the old regime he could claim ₹1,50,000 under Section 123, ₹25,000 under Section 126 and ₹50,000 of extra NPS, with no HRA or home loan. Which regime should he tell payroll to use?
options: Old regime, because he has three deductions
New regime, because his claims fall well short of the break-even amount
It makes no difference at this salary
Old regime, because the new regime does not allow a standard deduction
body.explanation: His claims total ₹2,25,000. At ₹20,00,000, the old regime needs about ₹7,09,000 of exemptions and deductions just to match the new regime. He would pay far more tax in the old regime, so he should stay in the default new regime and skip the declarations.

children.text: If the old regime does make sense for you, every claim needs evidence. Form 124 is the statement you give your employer listing each claim, backed by the documents below.

body.caption: Claims and the proof payroll will ask for

cells: Rent receipts or agreement, landlord's name and address, landlord's PAN if annual rent exceeds ₹1,00,000, and your relationship with the landlord
Travel tickets and boarding passes for the journey
Interest certificate from the lender, with the lender's name, address and PAN
PPF passbook, ELSS statement, life insurance premium receipts, tuition fee receipts, principal repayment in the lender's certificate
NPS transaction statement showing your own contribution
Premium receipts showing who is covered

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Landlord PAN Rule
body.textWithBlank: To claim HRA, you must give payroll your landlord's PAN once the rent you pay in a year exceeds ₹___.
body.explanation: Once annual rent crosses ₹1,00,000 (just ₹8,334 a month or more), the landlord's PAN is required. That PAN lets the department match your HRA claim against the rent your landlord reports.

children.text: HRA: the one claim worth calculating carefully
HRA exemption is the smallest of three amounts. "Salary" here means basic pay plus dearness allowance that forms part of retirement benefits.

body.latex: \text{HRA exempt} = \min\big(\text{HRA received},\ \text{Rent paid} - 10\%\text{ of salary},\ 50\%\text{ or }40\%\text{ of salary}\big)
body.caption: 50% in the eight metro cities, 40% everywhere else

body.text: From tax year 2026-27, the Income-tax Rules, 2026 treat eight cities as metros for HRA: Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Ahmedabad. Before this, only the first four qualified for the 50% limit. If you rent in one of the four new metros, your exemption may have jumped this year.

body.caption: Rahul's HRA in Bengaluru: basic ₹7,50,000, HRA received ₹3,75,000, rent ₹40,000 a month

children.text: Bengaluru's move to metro status raises Rahul's exemption by ₹75,000. In his 20% slab, that saves about ₹15,600 of tax a year, without a single rupee of extra rent.

body.title: Try It: HRA in a Non-Metro City
body.prompt: Kavya, a lecturer in Jaipur, has basic salary of ₹4,80,000 a year, receives HRA of ₹1,92,000 and pays rent of ₹18,000 a month. She is in the old regime. How much of her HRA is exempt?
body.explanation: Jaipur is not one of the eight metros, so the limit is 40%. The three amounts are: HRA received ₹1,92,000; rent ₹2,16,000 minus 10% of salary (₹48,000) = ₹1,68,000; and 40% of salary = ₹1,92,000. The smallest is ₹1,68,000, so ₹24,000 of her HRA stays taxable.

body.text: Inflated or invented rent receipts are easy to catch. Your landlord's PAN and your relationship with them now go on record, and rent paid to a parent or spouse is only valid if they actually own the property and report the rent as income. The department can match these claims against your landlord's return and AIS, and misreporting income carries heavy penalties on top of the tax.

children.text: Back to Rahul. In April he declared HRA of ₹3,75,000 plus ₹2,75,000 of deductions: ₹1,50,000 under Section 123, ₹50,000 of extra NPS, ₹25,000 for his own health cover and ₹50,000 for his senior citizen parents. In January he could prove only ₹1,10,000 under Section 123 (₹90,000 of EPF deducted through payroll and ₹20,000 of ELSS, not the ₹80,000 he had planned), and he had never bought his parents' policy.

body.caption: Rahul, old regime: declared vs proven

stats.label: TDS in February and March
stats.context: The whole shortfall squeezed into two months

body.caption: The unproven claims cost him no extra tax over the year compared with never declaring them, but they crushed his last two paychecks

children.text: Even after the shortfall, Rahul's old-regime tax of ₹94,120 is still slightly below the ₹97,500 he would pay in the new regime, thanks to his large HRA. His choice was right. His declarations were not.

body.title: Scenario: Proofs Missed the Deadline
body.scenario: Swati, an operations lead in Hyderabad, is in the old regime. She genuinely paid ₹1,50,000 into PPF and ELSS and ₹25,000 in health insurance premiums during the tax year, but she was travelling during the proof window and uploaded nothing. Payroll removed all her deductions and recovered the extra TDS in February and March. Her Form 130 shows no Section 123 or 126 deductions.
body.prompt: Has Swati lost these deductions? What should she do?
body.modelAnswer: No. Payroll's cut-off only decides how much TDS is deducted during the year. The deductions belong to her tax return, not to her employer. When she files her return for tax year 2026-27, she can claim ₹1,50,000 under Section 123 and ₹25,000 under Section 126 in the old regime, because the payments were made within the tax year. Her total tax falls, and the excess TDS comes back as a refund. She should keep the PPF passbook, ELSS statement and premium receipts, because a claim that does not match her Form 130 can prompt a query. Next year, she should upload proofs before the cut-off so her money is not locked up until the refund arrives.

body.title: Get Declarations Right This Year
steps: Add up the HRA exemption, home loan interest and deductions you can realistically claim, and compare with the break-even table before choosing a regime
If the new regime wins, choose it and skip declarations, except checking whether your employer offers NPS contributions
If the old regime wins, declare only amounts you will actually pay before 31 March
Collect your landlord's PAN now if your rent is above ₹1,00,000 a year
Set a reminder a week before your employer's proof cut-off and upload everything with Form 124
After March, compare your Form 130 with your records and claim anything missed in your return

cards.definition: Your estimate of rent, investments and payments for the year, given to payroll in April. It sets TDS until proofs are submitted.
Statement of claims for HRA, LTA, home loan interest and deductions, with evidence, submitted to your employer. Formerly Form 12BB.
Where the HRA exemption now sits in the Income-tax Act, 2025. Formerly Section 10(13A).
Deduction for home loan interest, up to ₹2,00,000 a year for a self-occupied house in the old regime. Formerly Section 24(b).
Deduction of up to ₹1,50,000 for EPF, PPF, ELSS, life insurance and similar items in the old regime. Formerly Section 80C.
NPS deductions. Employer contributions are allowed in both regimes. Your own extra contribution under 124(3) is old regime only. Formerly Section 80CCD.
Deduction for health insurance premiums in the old regime. Formerly Section 80D.
From tax year 2026-27: Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Ahmedabad, each eligible for the 50% limit.

points: April declarations set your TDS. January proofs confirm it, and any shortfall is recovered from your February and March salaries
Declarations only matter in the old regime, so compare your realistic claims with the break-even amount before choosing
At a ₹20,00,000 salary, the old regime needs roughly ₹7,09,000 of exemptions and deductions just to match the new regime
HRA exemption is the smallest of HRA received, rent minus 10% of salary, and 50% (metro) or 40% of salary
Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Ahmedabad are metros for HRA from tax year 2026-27, which can raise exemptions for renters there
Missing payroll's proof deadline does not forfeit a genuine deduction. You can still claim it in your return and get the excess TDS refunded

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax, legal or investment advice. Examples assume resident individuals below 60 with no surcharge and no income other than salary. Limits and provisions reflect the position understood at the time of writing and can change.
